title: Consistent Hashing
oneLine: Map keys and virtual nodes onto a ring so membership changes move only a bounded portion of data instead of remapping everything.
opening: Modulo hashing works while the server count is fixed, but adding or removing a server remaps most keys and can cause a cache miss or data migration storm. With consistent hashing, I hash both keys and virtual nodes into the same circular space and assign each key to the next node clockwise. Membership changes move only the keys in the affected interval. I would use many weighted virtual nodes per physical node to smooth distribution, reflect heterogeneous capacity, and make rebalancing gradual. I would still monitor skew because a ring does not eliminate hot keys, and I would separate placement metadata from application routing so membership updates are versioned and safe.
ask: Are we placing cached objects, durable data replicas, partitions, or requests?
What replication and failure-domain rules must placement obey?
scale: With N evenly distributed nodes, adding one node moves roughly 1/(N+1) of keys in the ideal case.
Use tens to hundreds of virtual nodes per physical node, then tune from observed variance and metadata cost.
Replica placement must skip the same host/AZ/rack; clockwise copies alone are not enough.

decisions.default: Use a ring when range movement and ordered tokens are useful; consider rendezvous hashing for simpler top-K node selection.
decisions.why: Both minimize remapping, but operational and lookup characteristics differ.
decisions.switch: Use a directory/range map when you need precise manual splits, ordered scans, or shard-specific policy.

decisions.default: Use weighted virtual nodes and rebalance incrementally.
decisions.why: They smooth random gaps and let a larger server own proportionally more ranges.
decisions.switch: Use a bounded-load variant when strict maximum imbalance matters.

decisions.default: Use a versioned, strongly consistent control-plane view.
decisions.why: Two clients routing with incompatible rings can create split ownership and inconsistent writes.
decisions.switch: Gossip can distribute health quickly, but ownership changes still need safe epochs/fencing.

deepDives.title: Replication
points: Walk clockwise to distinct failure domains, not merely distinct tokens.
Use preference lists and sloppy quorum/hinted handoff if availability is prioritized.
Record ownership epoch to reject writes from stale routers.

deepDives.title: Rebalancing
points: Stream ranges in throttled chunks while serving reads.
Dual-read or forward requests during ownership transfer.
Verify checksums before switching authoritative ownership.

failures.response: More virtual nodes, weighted tokens, bounded-load placement, and continuous skew metrics.

failures.risk: Hot key despite even key count
failures.response: Replicate/split the key, add request coalescing, or isolate a celebrity tenant; hashing balances keys, not workload.
Epoch numbers, fencing tokens, retry with latest topology, and controlled membership transitions.
Topology-aware placement across host, rack/AZ, and region.

questions.a: When N changes, most keys get a different remainder. Consistent hashing keeps unaffected intervals stable and moves only a fraction of keys.
They reduce uneven gaps, make capacity weighting possible, and break a physical node’s ownership into small movable pieces.

questions.q: Does consistent hashing guarantee perfect balance?
questions.a: No. It gives probabilistic balance and limited remapping. You still need enough tokens, workload metrics, and hot-key mitigation.

questions.q: How do clients discover the ring?
questions.a: From a versioned control plane or routing service. Cache locally, refresh on topology errors, and include an epoch so stale routing is detectable.

mistakes: Claiming only one key moves when a node joins
Ignoring virtual nodes and capacity weighting
Assuming balanced key count means balanced CPU or traffic
seniorSignal: Distinguish data placement, request routing, and membership consensus. Explain epochs, transfer safety, replica topology, and hot-key behavior.
implementation: Sorted map of 64-bit tokens for a ring
Weighted virtual nodes derived from node capacity
Topology metadata in etcd/Consul/ZooKeeper with epochs
Consistent-hash load balancing in Envoy or client SDK for request routing
